name: Island of Gorée
subtitle: A cultural property on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1978.

parts.text: UNESCO describes the property in these words: “The island of Gorée lies off the coast of Senegal, opposite Dakar. From the 15th to the 19th century, it was the largest slave-trading centre on the African coast. Ruled in succession by the Portuguese, Dutch, English and French, its architecture is characterized by the contrast between the grim slave-quarters and the elegant houses of the slave traders. Today it continues to serve as a reminder of human exploitation and as a sanctuary for reconciliation.”
Gorée is a small island about 900 metres long and 350 metres wide, two kilometres out to sea from the harbour of Dakar.
It is the smallest and least populated of Dakar's 19 districts, with 1,680 residents at the 2013 census.
The best-known building is the House of Slaves, built around 1776 by Nicolas Pépin, brother of the signare Anne Pépin. It became a museum in 1962 under the curator Boubacar Joseph Ndiaye.
It is visited by roughly 200,000 people a year, according to the same article, and Nelson Mandela, Pope John Paul II and Barack Obama are among the visitors it lists.

items.text: The Portuguese establish a presence on the island.
The Dutch arrive and build forts.
A brief period of English control.
Two periods of British occupation, during and after wars with France.

parts.text: Historians disagree about how many people were held or shipped from Gorée, and about what the House of Slaves can show.
Ndiaye, the museum's first curator, claimed that more than a million enslaved people passed through the house. Supporters later argued for as many as 15 million.
The historian Philip D. Curtin's research, as the Wikipedia article reports it, records 180,000 enslaved Africans transported from the French posts in Senegambia between 1711 and 1810.
A 2004 press article quotes Curtin estimating that about 50,000 people may have spent time on the island over four centuries, and saying that it was never a key departure point.
Wikipedia's article on the island gives a figure of no more than 500 people a year.

The same press article reports that the House of Slaves was built in 1775–1778 as a merchant's home, and quotes Curtin saying that the rocks around the Door of No Return are too many for boats to dock there.
It also quotes the museum curator Abdoulaye Camara as saying the house gives "a distorted account" meant for tourists.
The historian Ana Lucia Araujo is quoted in Wikipedia's article as saying it is "not a real place from where real people left in the numbers they say".

gaps: A scholarly history of Senegambia, to replace Wikipedia and the press article for the numbers. Curtin (1969) is named but has not been read here.
Senegalese historians' position and the view of the museum today, beyond one curator quoted in a 2004 article.
Another figure appears in the House of Slaves article, 26,000 people recorded as passing through the island, without a clear source in what was read.
UNESCO's longer statement of why the island was inscribed (the open-data record has a justification text that has not been used here).
